caste.quote: Each baiting station was composed of 50-ml Falcon tube loosely stuffed with pieces of paper towel to trap foraging workers at the opening of the tube.

Each individual worker collected from the baits was placed in a 1.5-ml Eppendorf tube with clay plugged in the cap to prevent ants from hiding in the coolest space of the tube (Bujan & Kaspari, 2017).
The morphological measurements were taken on at least three individual workers or minors for each species (Gaudard et al., 2019).

basisOfRecord.quote: Ants were sampled from two habitats, that is, secondary forest and rubber plantation.

To sample species assemblage for each habitat and compare species trait responses to land use change, field sites were chosen within representative secondary forests and rubber plantations within the Trang Province (Figure S1).

To collect a sufficient number of foraging individuals per species from both rubber plantations and forests to measure their morphological and thermal traits, baiting method was used as it allows to attract large numbers of alive individuals (Roeder et al., 2018) and accounts for the taxonomic diversity encountered to perform species assemblage comparison (Andersen et al., 2002; Brassard et al., 2021).

Each individual worker collected from the baits was placed in a 1.5-ml Eppendorf tube with clay plugged in the cap to prevent ants from hiding in the coolest space of the tube (Bujan & Kaspari, 2017).

measurementStatistic.quote: The results showed that both physiological and morphological traits may explain, although unevenly, the differences observed in ant assemblages between forest and rubber plantation.
Conspecific Critical Thermal maximum (CT max ) in different habitats for (a) *Anoplolepis gracilipes* and (b) *Odontoponera denticulata*.
Trait Probability Density (TPD) of CT max of (c) *A. gracilipes* and (d) *O. denticulata.*

Lower part: $\mathsf { C T _ { m a x } }$ of ant species from forest (red section) and rubber plantation (blue section) with p value of nonparametric Mann–Whitney U test of species average $\mathsf { C T } _ { \mathsf { m a x } }$ difference between the two habitats, and the dash lines indicate the mean value of $\mathsf { C T } _ { \mathsf { m a x } }$ across species in each habitat.

Our results show that foraging ants in rubber planta tions present higher thermal tolerance than those in forests (Figures 2 and S3) and a shift in the trait probability distribution of ant assemblages suggesting a loss of ants with lower $\mathsf { C T } _ { \mathsf { m a x } }$ but a gain of species able to tolerate higher temperature in rubber plantation habitat.
